headline: Go services, and the production work that keeps them fast, for the tools support teams rely on.
pitch: I lead a team of three engineers at DGRS Labs and run all of its infrastructure myself, from Linux servers to CI/CD. loom, the Go multi-agent runtime I built there, runs agents concurrently and streams live events to shared sessions. Before that I led delivery of a USSD loan service on a platform serving 16 million customers in six countries.

matches.evidence: loom and buckt are both Go. loom is the orchestration platform behind CoNexus, coordinating six agents per scene with followers run concurrently; buckt manages the platform's media library in production.
Cut API response times from 1.2s to 600ms and database reads by 40%, and took average page loads from 4.5s to 1.1s. At Equity the loan service handled over 1 million loan requests a month.

matches.requirement: SQL and NoSQL databases, especially Cassandra
matches.evidence: PostgreSQL is my default, and I've used Redis for caching and session state in production. I haven't run Cassandra in production; that would be new ground.

links.label: Redis sessions in the USSD framework

matches.evidence: As the sole owner of DGRS Labs' infrastructure, keeping it up is my job. I built its backup and disaster-recovery system, and owned production support through Equity's rollouts across six countries.

matches.requirement: Well-tested code and high quality standards
matches.evidence: Set up separate dev, staging and production environments with release rules the team follows, and a generator–reviewer workflow with production-like Docker test environments. loom ships with its own test harness.

resume.summary: Lead software engineer with 5+ years building and running production backends in Golang, Python and Rust. Leads a team of three at an AI studio, built its Go agent orchestration platform, and single-handedly runs its infrastructure and CI/CD. Previously led delivery of a USSD loan service on a financial platform serving 16 million customers in six countries.

note:
Support tooling is where a backend's speed and reliability reach people directly. When it's slow, a support agent and a customer are both left waiting. That's the kind of system I like building, and most of my recent work has been in Go.

At DGRS Labs I own the whole path from code to production: the services, the database work, the pipelines, and the recovery plan for when something breaks. I'd bring that habit of owning what I ship, and of thinking about how it fails before it does.

Cassandra would be new to me. I've gone deep on PostgreSQL and Redis, and I'd want to learn Cassandra properly on real traffic. The systems linked above have live demos if you'd like to try them.
